item.title: The Black Swan
item.description:
• One single observation can invalidate a general statement derived from millennia of confirmatory sightings of millions of white swans.
  • Black Swan Even
    • Outlier: Outside of regular expectation because past events didn’t forecast it.
    • Extreme Impact: If it was mild, it wouldn’t be that important.
    • Explanation after the event (Retrospective): Human mind finds explanations to make it predictable afterwards.
  • What you know cannot really hurt you.
  • Not understanding the black swan events will lead you to a faulty future prediction. So, we need to focus somehow on what we do not know.
  • One who knows how to strategize differently might easily beat those who study strategies but don’t invent new ones.
  • Though we don’t care about the extremes of personalities, that’s where the major and big problems come from; even when they are rare.
  • One should avoid using terms made of knowledge to describe not-knowing.
  • There can be no knowing except that your map is not the territory. If you over-analyze, you again fall into the same pit.
  • Knowing the grayness of ideas, theories, philosophies can be a robust way to tackle black swan events.

Quotes

This goes to Information encoding as well. If everyone knows about the strategy, it’s not a strategy.

item.title: Zen and Art of Motorcycle Maintenance
item.description:
Quotes

We want to make good time, but for us now this is measured with emphasis on ‘good’ rather than ‘time’ and when you make that shift in emphasis the whole approach changes.

In a car you’re always in a compartment, and because you’re used to it you don’t realize that through that car window everything you see is just more TV. You’re a passive observer and it is all moving by you boringly in a frame. On a cycle the frame is gone. You’re completely in contact with it all. You’re in the scene, not just watching it anymore, and the sense of presence is overwhelming.

item.title: The Beginning of Infinity
item.description:
Author: David Deutsch

Completed on: 2025-01-04

Summary

Good Explanations

  • Deutsch attributes all progress, both theoretical and practical, to quest for good explanations.
  • Good explanations go far beyond extrapolations from experience of the creators.
  • Unique thing about humans is the ability to create good explanations. Everyrhing we do to improve our lives attributes to this ability.
  • The real source of our theories is conjecture, and the real source of our knowledge is conjecture alternating with criticism. We create theories by rearranging, combining,altering and adding to existing ideas with the intention of improving upon them. The role of experiment and observation is to choose between existing theories, not to be the source of new ones.
    • In fact this is the main thing about innovation in general: there is no rational definition of where to look for answers or good questions. And there is no bad theory as long as our main basis for it is criticism with proper logic.
  • They even go beyond biological knowledge which has limited reach. Another difference is that mutations are random; conjectures are intentional.
  • We have known the world both to be more bigger and violent, but also awesome in detail. And the more we get good explanations, the elegance increases as well.
  • Good explanations make it harder to even fool yourselves. Its hard to vary it specifically for cases it doesn’t work with. And since it has an autonomous meaning and autonomous domain of applicability.
    • e.g. It might touch in places where you don’t even want it to touch and if its a good explanation, it will work there effectively as well.
    • That’s what is up with autonomic nature of it.
  • Old ways of thought, which did not seek good explanations, permitted no process such as science for correcting errors and misconceptions. Improvements happened so rarely that most people never experienced one. Ideas were static for long periods. Being bad explanations, even the best of them typically had little reach and were therefore brittle and unreliable beyond, and often within, their traditional applications.
  • We need to understand the contradictory ideas together in one piece: we will never run out of problems but we will keep creating good explanations and improve on our ability to do so at an exponential pace too.

Philosophical Ideas and Contrasts

  • Empiricism was the first basis from where our experimental science as we know today started.
  • We haven’t experienced Big Bang or billion light years; yet we have good explanations of it. With Inductivism ,we couldn’t have even understood about the stars and the universe except the fact that they are just dots.
  • Then comes the idea of Fallibilism
  • One good question he asks is why did our ancestors not have the same understanding we had although they had same brains and eyes like us anatomically. Its not for their lack of trying, nor for their lack of thinking. But they never could understand what’s beneath that appearance. He attributes it to this: They wanted to create knowledge, in order to make progress, but they did not know how.
  • This is why the Royal Society (one of the earliest scientific academies, founded in London in 1660) took as its motto ‘Nullius in verba’, which means something like ‘Take no one’s word for it’.
  • Galileo Galilei understood the importance of experimental tests as distinct from other forms of experiment and observation, which is modern day understanding of repeatability and testability. Popper called it criterion of demarcation between science and non-science.
  • Solving a problem requires an explanation: a statement of the reality that accounts for the appearance.
  • Ancient accounts of reality started with Anthropocentric theories. One one end is “Principle of Mediocrity” which is the exact opposite of anthropocentrism that there is nothing significant about humans in cosmic sense. These theories are equally dangerous if accepted as maxims.

Scientific Attitude

  • Two apparent viable theories making conflicting predictions to be distinguished by experiment.
  • Takes a great deal of conjecture, criticism and testing to understand that stars in the sky need fuel as well as are in free fall, even though they don’t seem to fall to earth as well as light up for timelines as huge as billions of years.
  • Rejecting erroneous data, amending it etc. happen concurrently with scientific discovery. Even the (why, how, what) to look for as critical data is also told by the theory.
  • By finding data that contradicts our explanations, we understand that our explanations are not good.
    • Greek myth of winter onset disproved by knowing that one part of Earth has summer while another one has winter and vice versa.
    • And these bad explanations like winter happening because Demeter is sad is very easy to vary. It could be because Zeus is sad or something along those lines.
    • Advocating a particular theory in preference to the others is irrational when we have two theories that can account equally well for the phenomenon they are trying to explain. But if that applies to other places like usual good explanations, then that’s where we might find one to be a better explanation than the other.
  • This idea is a challenge for science in general and one that Richard Feynmann also teaches us. If you think Scientific theories as absolute truths, you are also a liar. They are the best explanations of reality for the time being and should always be subject to scrutiny for better explanations. And regarding which theory can explain it, there is no rational or right answer to it, though many try to say so.
  • Bad explanations don’t become good by changing them a bit after being proved wrong by experiment.
  • Authority should never be a basis for why we adopt a theory. Not even the scientific ones.
  • A theory is a good explanation when its hard to vary, and that’s very essential to Science.
  • Instrumentalism considers explanation unnecessary, and so do any random theory that people preach based on authority alone.
  • Very little in nature is detectable by unaided human senses. Most of what happens is too fast or too slow, too big or too small, or too remote, or hidden behind opaque barriers, or operate on principles too different from anything that influenced our evolution. But in some cases, we can arrange for such phenomena to become perceptible, via scientific instruments.
    • Today, most telescopes are not even for human eyes.
    • In one way, instruments are bringing us closer to reality. In another way, they are pushing away from physicality of reality. Most observations are theory-heavy. Most observations are indirect. Most errors are errors in explanations.
  • In the terms that Science assumes that we cannot know the world completely can lead to extremely bad explanations.
  • Explaining the world led us to controlling it.
  • More advanced the technology, shorter the gap between inspiration and automation.
  • Scientists critic, reject a lot of bad explanations inside their minds.

Spaceship Earth Metaphor

  • Spaceship Earth Metaphor assumes that our creativity might just perish outside of Earth, and only is possible because of Earth.
    • The most fundamental assumption is access to matter for creativity to continue.
    • Matter, Energy is abundant in the universe for us to be able to create good explanations.
  • Biosphere is also a death trap for humans rather than just life support system. It’s notoriously cruel to individuals. Average rate of extinction since the beginning of life in Earth has been about 10 species per year. And mass extinction events. We made this biosphere safe for us.

Fine Tuning Theory

  • Brandon Carter in 1974 calculated that if strength of interaction between charged particles were a few percent smaller, no planets or any huge objects would have formed. If it were a little greater, no stars would ever explode. So, no complex chemistry, and no life based on these assumptions.
    • The objection to this is that we are not sure if chemistry or planets are necessary to form life at all.
    • And that posits to the possibility of parallel universes where these values are instantiated differently as well.
  • Sciama says that if the value of these constants are close to optimal values for creating astrophysicists, then it would statistically refute anthropic explanation for the value. He concludes that universe is only just capable of producing astrophysicists when more constants are involved. because the amount of constants involved isn’t known.
    • That turns out to be a bad explanation because we don’t know the difference in same laws with different constants to different laws of physics. And there are infinitely many different possible laws of physics.
    • If laws of physics exist in one form with constants differing between parallel universes, then anthropic explanation should explain why different laws were not instantiated.
  • Before a discovery is made, no predictive process could reveal the content or the consequences of that discovery. So scientific discovery is profoundly unpredictable, despite the fact that it is determined by the laws of physics.

Abstractions

  • As with the force of gravity, our best explanation denies that it exists, then we must stop assuming that it does.
  • Emergence are those explanations which are resolved at higher quasi autonomous level, and almost self-contained. Like explaining AI.
  • This is in regards to the fact that Reductionism cannot always explain every phenomenon. That’s why Emergence is important for some good explanations.
  • Second law of thermodynamics says that high-level physical processes tend towards ever greater disorder. We can say this on high-level but when looking at atoms colliding with each other, abiding by laws of physics, is not enough to derive second law of thermodynamics. But this is the question: Does having theory of everything make reductionism true?
  • So, there are explanations on many levels and they imply to one another from top to bottom and imply many explanations between each other. But for creation of knowledge, it consists of emergent phenomenon.
  • Removing gravity as entity doesn’t mean we discard the a lot of facts about motion of planets and so on. Its an abstraction we put in for good explanation.
  • A computer program beating you at chess doesn’t mean silicon atoms or the computer. Explanation of that behavior is explained at an abstract level of computer programs which are not physically real.
  • The very idea of cause is emergent and abstract. This is in relation to example given by Donald Hofstadter on Domino Network.
  • Often times, our explanations discard lots of low level details, create an abstract simplified version of that physical phenomenon, and explains it. It’s as if we experience reality in analog and create explanations on discrete form. Quantization happens in between the process.
  • Beauty, right and wrong, primality, infinite sets – they all exist objectively. But not physically. What does that mean? Certainly they can affect you – as examples like Hofstadter’s show – but apparently not in the same sense that physical objects do.
  • Sets of phenomena that can be explained well in terms of each other without analysing them into their constituent entities such as atoms.

Enlightenment

  • Environment where the space for good explanations and criticisms on them is heavily supported
  • British Enlightenment was well aware of human fallibility, and worked for continuous good explanations.
    • It built institutions that did not hinder slow yet continuous upgrades of good explanations because it understood human Fallibility. Worked for small improvements that they didn’t know how it would span out in the future as well.
  • Athens was defeated by Sparta in 404 BCE and then got authoritarian government. Soon after, it got freedom back. But the open-ended progress that it had before Spartans took control wasn’t there anymore. The optimism was gone.
  • Problems are inevitable, because our knowledge will always be infinitely far from complete. Some problems are hard, but it is a mistake to confuse hard problems with problems unlikely to be solved. Problems are soluble, and each particular evil is a problem that can be solved. An optimistic civilization is open and not afraid to innovate, and is based on traditions of criticism. Its institutions keep improving, and the most important knowledge that they embody is knowledge of how to detect and eliminate errors. There may have been many short-lived enlightenments in history. Ours has been uniquely long-lived.
  • At the time of Medici, artists in Florence were able to show anything that they considered beautiful, and invent new styles. After the first time they were gone, even when they came for second time, the optimism was gone. It seems that its very fragile.
  • SOCRATES: Bah! I ask you in return: are you a benevolent or a malevolent god? If benevolent, then what do I have to fear? If malevolent, then I disdain to fear you.
  • Socrates hates a situation where he is perfectly secure in his beliefs. He says one can tell that conditions are good for seeing when one can easily see what is there.
  • Any civilization where its not open to suggestions, where you cannot criticize ideas, where you cannot seek truth because they think they already have truth is what we don’t want to end up at.
  • The very idea that improvements are possible implies that there are inadequacies in current set of ideas. Knowledge held immune from criticism never can be improved.
  • What matters in all cases is the explanation you create, within your own mind, for the facts, and for the observations and advice in question.
  • All knowledge originates from same source as dreams, which is within ourselves. Your guesses.
  • We want true explanations. So we seek explanations that remain robust when we test them against those flickers and shadows, and against each other, and against criteria of logic and reasonableness and everything else we can think of.
  • Difference that Plato sees between Athenians and Spartans :
    • Kids daring to ask anything
    • Honours dead poets, don’t honour living ones because living ones can write anything new anytime.
    • No philosophers
  • A philosopher as a king can make that difference to make those beneath him understand this optimism and progress.
  • The default assumption should be that misunderstandings are ubiquitous and that neither intelligence nor the intention to be accurate is any guarantee against them.
  • All theories and explanations are cumulative and often times the expounding work is much better than original theory like Einstein’s theory of relativity would be when explained by his paper alone.
  • Scientists are not interested in who originated the theory, not in opinions of who wrote it etc.

Universal Explanations

  • As long as the system has the highest valued symbol, it’s not universal. So, it cannot be generalized. e.g. Tallying

Mathematics

  • Seeking perfect system of mathematics without logical consistency is in a way form of justificationism. The object of mathematics is to understand and explain abstract entities. And it only has to be about good explanations, nothing more than that.
  • Finitism is also studied in maths.
  • Cantors paradox gives a good example on thinking about infinity.
  • The intuitive notion of proportion and Probability doesn’t work with infinities.
  • Then Godel’s incompleteness theorem cleaned it up about this space of infinity that we have based on “unprovable” theorems, “undecidable” problems.
  • There is nothing mathematically special about the undecidable questions, the non-computable functions, the unprovable propositions. They are distinguished by physics only. Different physical laws would make different things infinite, different things computable, different truths – both mathematical and scientific – knowable. It is only the laws of physics that determine which abstract entities and relationships are modelled by physical objects such as mathematicians’ brains, computers and sheets of paper.
  • Whether a mathematical proposition is true or not is indeed independent of physics. But the proof of such a proposition is a matter of physics only.
  • Mathematical truth is absolutely necessary and transcendent, but all knowledge is generated by physical processes, and its scope and limitations are conditioned by the laws of nature.
  • The whole motivation for seeking perfect foundation for Mathematics was mistaken. The object of mathematics is to understand abstract entities. Mathematics is there to seek good explanations too.
  • So there is something special – infinitely special, it seems – about the laws of physics as we actually find them, something exceptionally computation-friendly, prediction-friendly and explanation-friendly. The physicist Eugene Wigner called this ‘the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences’.
  • Classically computable problems don’t mean that there isn’t more.
  • Even unprovable mathematical explanations can be interesting and continue to be useful. And a lot of these explanations are not computable by classical computers but that’s us limited by Physics. Undecidability today no more contradicts the maxim that problems are soluble than does the fact that there are truths about the physical world that we shall never know.
  • Proof is a physical process: whether a mathematical proposition is provable or unprovable, decidable or undecidable, depends on the laws of physics, which determine which abstract entities and relationships are modelled by physical objects. Similarly, whether a task or pattern is simple or complex depends on what the laws of physics are.

Optimism

  • Possibilities in future are infinite. We just saw that even the big hole in mathematics can be solved someday.
  • So, we have to keep solving problems and will be facing better and bigger problems.
  • Trying to know the unknowable leads inexorably to error and self-deception. Among other things, it creates a bias towards pessimism.
  • Both the original ‘optimism’ and the original ‘pessimism’ are close to pure pessimism as I shall define it.
  • There is no precaution that can be taken, no perfect future, but it keeps getting flown with universality and better explanations.
  • A lot of times our better explanations solve even the problems that could have wiped us easily. e.g. Population Explosion, Meteorite Strike or things like that.
  • Objective progress is indeed possible in politics just as it is in morality generally and in science.
  • Thus the very question ‘Who should rule?’ begs for violent, authoritarian answers, and has often received them. But the entire stance is based on Fallibilism and if we understand that policies are always going to be flawed and also assume that they can be improved upon, thats all we need.
  • All evils are caused by insufficient knowledge.

Humans

  • Humans derive Insight even from mindless works during theoretical research and this is one of the fundamental differences between a human and a robot.
  • Using knowledge to cause automated physical transformations is not unique to humans. All organisms keep themselves alive using this.
    • Every cell is a chemical factory.
    • Human differs in how it can use explanatory knowledge instead of rule-of-thumb and how they create this knowledge ( conjecture, criticism of ideas) rather than variation and selection of genes.
    • Basically as if we improvised the genetic algorithm itself. Maybe not perfect, but we keep getting better and better.
    • That’s why humans transform the inhospitable environments like the biosphere to be support system for themselves.
  • Humans are universal constructors.
  • We don’t become less of a human by losing a limb.
  • Something is definitely finite if it could in principle be encompassed by human experience but what does it mean to “experience” something? Was Cantor experiencing infinity when he proved theorems about it? Or was he experiencing only symbols? But we only ever experience symbols.

Sustenance of creativity

  • Even life spans might get longer as we eliminate more disease and ageing in the future.
  • In biology, DNA and all other biochemical molecules could be synthesized and experimented on. And, although biology field trips would be difficult (because the closest natural ecosystem would be millions of light years away), arbitrary life forms could be created and studied in artificial ecosystems, or in virtual-reality simulations of them.
  • One can explain supernova without mentioning people or knowledge at all. That brews against the anthropocentric explanations.
    • Yeah until there is no sign of intelligence acting, there is a pattern to be understood. But once we know that intelligence exists in abundance, all our theories are subject to tremendous doubt because these could be pendulums of higher intelligence.
  • We don’t even have a language to what happens to us if we are in the point-blank range of a supernovae explosion.
  • Experimentalists call “proxy” as this: a physical variable that can be measured as a way of measuring another variable. e.g. Cork from a champagne at SETI is opened if we know that extraterrestial intelligence exists.
    • Non-explanatory systems cannot cross the conceptual gap that an explanatory conjecture crosses, to engage with unexperienced evidence or non-existent phenomena. Nor is that true only of fundamental science: if such-and-such a load were put on the proposed bridge it would collapse, says the engineer, and such statements can be true and immensely valuable even if the bridge is never even built, let alone subjected to such a load.
  • There are unimaginably many environments doing nothing at all and generating evidence for us to study.
  • Mistaking appearance for reality, or local regularities for universal laws.
  • So, there is a good chance that it will sustain pretty easily since we have access to what’s needed very almost infinitely throughout the universe.

Knowledge Creation

  • Human brains generate knowledge by varying conjecture and selecting based on criticism and experiment. Genetic adaptations do it by variation of existing information, alternating with selection.
  • Biological knowledge is non-explanatory: thus limited in reach. Human knowledge can have unlimited reach.
  • Biological knowledge with mutations is random. Conjectures are intentional.
  • If we really think in detail, biological adaptations seem to be more below optimal than human explanations. e.g. Blind spots in eye contradict the functional design goal of an eye.
  • Future unlimited creation of knowledge contradicts creationism because if the trend continues, we might have full functioning simulations soon enough.
  • Evolution can create designs without a designer though it might not be efficient about it.
  • A good design is hard to vary: If the different parts had been differently shaped from what they are, of a different size from what they are, or placed after any other manner, or in any other order, than that in which they are placed, either no motion at all would have been carried on in the machine, or none which would have answered the use that is now served by it.
  • Just from experience, knowledge doesn’t seem to be derivable at all. If it was the case, our ancestors who were looking at the skies like we were would have figured it out already. Instead, truth is that knowledge must first be guessed and then tested.
  • Some genetic variations in the species make other variations significantly disappear because other can’t mate enough and produce enough offsprings. This is not selection of the best, yet it made that dysfunctional species continue. Genes don’t do much for individual, and in many cases not for the species survival as well.
  • The species and individuals have to suffer the consequences of selection pressure. So does a human society.
  • In addition, there is the phenomenon of reach: when the knowledge in a gene happens to have reach, it will help the individual to help itself in a wider range of circumstances, and by more, than the spreading of the gene strictly requires. That is why mules stay alive even though they are sterile.
  • The most important source of variation in explanatory theories is creativity. For instance, when people are trying to understand an idea that they hear from others, they typically understand it to mean what makes most sense to them, or what they are most expecting to hear, or what they fear to hear, and so on.

Universality

  • Language is based on sounds human voice can produce.
  • Writing system covers every possible word in that language, even the ones that haven’t been coined.
  • And indeed it seems to be a recurring theme in the early history of many fields that universality, when it was achieved, was not the primary objective, if it was an objective at all. A small change in a system to meet a parochial purpose just happened to make the system universal as well. This is the jump to universality.
  • Adding simple rules incrementally can make systems much more powerful.
  • You start by simple systems. Then by adding rules it gets complex. Then you strip out the complexity to make it simple, and there’s something universal about it.
  • Knowledge is information which, when it is physically embodied in a suitable environment, tends to cause itself to remain so.
  • Also, the idea of using humans as computers in Three Body Problem where one moves similar to other pieces is similar implementation of computation just using humans instead of transistors.
  • Not always is the universal thing just taken and used even if effective: Medieval Europe didn’t put Indian Numerals from the Arabs into use.
  • Greek culture might not have had concept of abstract number at all. That’s why universality was a very hard concept to grasp, let alone try to do something along those lines.
  • The jump to computational universality should have happened in the 1820s, when the mathematician Charles Babbage designed a device that he called the Difference Engine – a mechanical calculator which represented decimal digits by cogs, each of which could click into one of ten positions. Then Babbage thought of “Analytical Engine” one that would be capable of computing anything that ‘human’ computers could. It never came to be though the universal idea of computation in abstract terms was laid out in terms of mechanical parts. They had electric relays being used for telegraphy but didn’t use it for ideas on computation. If they had, everything that followed computational progress might have followed so much early on.
  • The mathematician and computer pioneer Alan Turing later called this mistake ‘Lady Lovelace’s objection’. It was not computational universality that Lovelace failed to appreciate, but the universality of the laws of physics. Science at the time had almost no knowledge of the physics of the brain.
  • Hofstadter and Lovelace both of them share the mistaken premise that low-level computational steps cannot possibly add up to a higher-level ‘I’ that affects anything. The difference between them is that they chose opposite horns of the dilemma that that poses: Lovelace chose the false conclusion that AI is impossible, while Hofstadter chose the false conclusion that no such ‘I’ can exist.
  • Tallying is universal only if it is digital. The limitation that the information must be digital doesn’t decrease value of universality of digital computers.
  • Because of the necessity for error-correction, all jumps to universality occur in digital systems. Nothing can represent tone of voice or elementary sound perfectly. This is one of the key ideas: not just in terms of science but Spirituality in general as well. Its as if being enlightened means giving up access to digital and just taking the information raw.
  • RNAs have been most successful replicators. They are like programming that uses these molecules as alphabet. At some time, system switched from RNA to DNA which is more stable for storing large amount of information. And it stopped there? The answer could be that it was universal already in terms of representation. Adleman in 1994 finally rediscovered this universal property: the experimental use of DNA as a computational system.

Artificial Creativity

  • Qualia is neither describable nor predictable. Not useful with scientific attitude.
  • Self-awareness or human abilities that are associated with AGI are very unscientific in terms of attitude.
  • Abstract emergent explanation doesn’t mean its not a good explanation. But that would not prevent it from being a good explanation. It would not have to account for the specific computational steps that composed a joke, just as the theory of evolution does not have to account for why every specific mutation succeeded or failed in the history of a given adaptation. This is one of the key ideas of modern day AI and Model Explainability that everyone keeps talking about.
  • It will explain itself in multi-dimensional interactions just like us. That’s the explainable good explanations we are talking about.
  • If AI fakes AI well enough, its deemed as achieved.
  • Once you automate every sub-problem of a robotic automation, and keep updating based on feedback, this requires less inspiration and more perspiration.
  • An AI should be capable of rewriting subroutines that a careful human programmer programmed into a working robot.

Infinity

  • Zeno’s paradox : Both physical laws and infinity exist in one place.
  • Human Experience which happens in analog form like human tones or sounds
  • In computation, Turing proved that there are indeed “non-computable” problems.

Evolution of Creativity

  • Creativity can only produce knowledge of any kind.
  • Closer observation would have revealed that human languages and the knowledge for human tool use were being transmitted through memes and not genes. So, memes became these better universal replicators than genes.
  • Creativity, though not prominently visible in earlier humans, must have been evolving there too. During the period when creativity was evolving, the ability to replicate memes was evolving too.
  • Once creativity and meme transmission are both present, they greatly enhance each other’s evolutionary value. And it made cumulative improvements ona timescale of generations.
  • Seems like small genetic improvement in creativity produced just one noticeable innovation and nothing more at the beginning. If it had grown too much, the reproduction of individuals with more ability to innovate would have been much faster. It probably started as functional advantage: creating displays to attract mates by colorful clothing, decorations, story-telling etc. and grew from there. Else, that wouldn’t have propagated. And we haven’t been able to reproduce this artificially.
  • A more plausible theory on why creativity got selected as sexual-selection was ability to create and gain status through social manipulation.
  • And innovations sometimes have reach: a new skill of making a string of decorative beads in one generation might become the skill of making a slingshot in the next. So why were practical innovations originally so rare? This is indeed the contradiction. Also interesting to question why certain animals though they show primitive versions of creativity can never amass much afterwards.
  • Memes cannot be observed inside other people’s brains or be downloaded. Ability to mimic others helped transmit those memes.
  • Theory has to come first. It has to be conjectured, not derived.
  • One needs to know the ideas before one can imitate the behaviour. So imitating behaviour cannot be how we acquire memes. What to imitate can be a very diverse thing that requires creativity on its own.
  • We have communicated really well our language, speech to the next generation.
  • Our assumptions come from us, and we judge them afterwards. Its not coming from outside, and we understand these. Its like our genes know it.
  • Mirror neurons help animals imitate each other’s behavior.
  • Parrots never have a choice about which sounds to imitate, or about what constitutes imitating them. We do. Parrot transmits memes but without understanding it. Without having a choice whether to transmit it or not.
  • Apes mimic by behavior parsing without creating any explanatory knowledge as well though it seems more like us than parrots. Apes cannot even parrot sounds.
  • Humans when acquiring memes are doing very different. They are parsing and making a lossy representation of it in their minds, and basically corroborating it the next time with their attributed explanatory knowledge that they had generated from that meme. Lossy copying in trying to understand thus creating a framework. this could be a potential idea to make ai work too.
  • Humans use conjecture, criticism and experiment to create good explanations of the meaning of things – other people’s behaviour, their own, and that of the world in general. Building this ball of knowledge I think is important with ai as well if we want to create true intelligence that’s without a doubt.
  • Human memes were replicated by creativity and creativity itself was evolving to replicate memes. So, it was a loop in itself. So, existing knowledge was being transmitted for the most part. And one who receives a meme had this challenge to discover a human explanation just like a human scientist needs to generate a good explanation for the phenomena. And that had to re-evaluated from that knowledge just like critics try to find errors on the existing theory with rigor.
  • We basically learn from trial and error.
  • In fact all creativity does, for no idea can be represented entirely explicitly. When we make an explicit conjecture, it has an inexplicit component whether we are aware of it or not. And so does all criticism.
  • First the memes were about practical things only like how to make food accessible. Creativity was required to replicate memes. As it became more important, memory capacity, finer motor control, brain structures to deal with language etc. might have developed. So, memetic information transfer increased from one generation to next. So did the complexity of memes.
  • Innovation could have been low in static societies even when the memetic capacity was increasing rapidly.
  • Memes evolve towards greater fidelity of replication.
  • Discovering the wish and expectations of those who are important in a tribe required some replication of behavior that was standard among them. It required creativity to thrive in static society that enabled one to be less innovative than others. But the question becomes: how do animals thrive without this creativity then?
  • Creativity is a property of software.
  • Hardware for practical creativity would be like memory capacity which helped one to remember more memes, enact more, and more accurately enact them.
  • Genes evolving hardware to support more and better memes, and memes evolving to take over ever more of what had previously been genetic functions such as choice of mate, and methods of eating, fighting and so on.
  • But the jump to universal explainer is very hard to understand. If we did, we could program one.
  • ‘Machiavellian hypothesis’ that human intelligence evolved in order to predict the behaviour of others, and to fool them. Seems like what we are doing with AI is exactly that, so we might be on the right track after all.
  • Blackmore’s meme machine idea is more reasonable because that explains the evolutionary need for creativity as well.
  • Not only is creativity necessary for human meme replication, it is also sufficient. Deaf people and blind people and paralysed people are still able to acquire and create human ideas to a more or less full extent. Maybe disabled adapted better when we got creative? So, its as if even the weakest individuals from species is also able to survive and thrive.
  • The beginning of creativity was, in that sense, the beginning of infinity.
  • The memes that creativity preserved is why we see the static societies. Times and again, we find ourselves out of it with Enlightenment.

Uncertainty

  • On the face of it, creativity cannot have been useful during the evolution of humans, because knowledge was growing much too slowly for the more creative individuals to have had any selective advantage.
  • Complex memes do not mandate specific bodily actions, but rules. We can see the actions, but not the rules, so how do we replicate them? We replicate them by creativity. That solves both problems, for replicating memes unchanged is the function for which creativity evolved. And that is why our species exists.
  • Sustain on one hand means to provide with what one needs. But it can also mean suppression of change, which is seldom what we need.
  • All disasters are caused by “poor resource management”.
  • The lack of problem solving ability of Easter Island is what we need to take as lesson more than anything else.
  • Scientific attitude would not have guaranteed their welfare, but it could have given them a chance.
  • In Guns, Germs, and Steel, author says that different continents evolved differently because of different geographies, plants, animals and micro-organisms. Goes on to say that the reason Americas never developed technological civilization before advent of Europeans was that no animals were there suitable for domestication. But same can be said for a lot of other places where technology didn’t appear automatically.
  • Polynesian enlightenment
  • If the ancient Greek enlightenment had continued, Athenians might have been the first to settle the Pacific islands and they would now be the ‘Polynesians’.
  • What if humans thought of riding mega faunas instead of driving them to extinction when they arrived in Americas?
  • Analysing any bit of biogeography across Asia, Europe, and America can teach us about Cold War.
  • Enlightenment wasn’t caused by territories. Instead, territories would get modified in case people there get enlightened. Knowledge converted landscape into resources.
  • Humans can find ways to improve by thinking but there is thinking that can make it stagnant too. So, ideas are what makes us thrive and get stale too.
  • The Easter Islanders failed to navigate their way off the island, just as the Romans failed to solve the problem of how to change governments peacefully.
  • Sustained creation of knowledge needs the scientific attitude: optimism brewed with a tradition of criticism.
  • When we think about future problems, we can’t necessarily predict the growth of good explanations which will help us navigate these future problems. So, we need to discount our fear with this understanding and thus be optimistic about the future.
  • People find new ways to have the same thing, same resource made in different way. e.g. We came to Lithium Ion to Lithium Polymer to Sodium batteries and will even improvise on that. So, if we just assume Lithium is going to end, we didn’t take into account our ability to create new better explanations.
  • People are problem-solvers: creators of the unsustainable solution and hence also of the next problem. Sustainability in that sense is the disease and people are the cure.
  • To expect that problems will always be solved in time to avert disasters would be the same fallacy. People often fail to understand a core fact that problems are inevitable. And there are new problems arising for civilizations that were never seen before like The Black Swan event.
  • The only rational policy, in all three cases, is to judge institutions, plans and ways of life according to how good they are at correcting mistakes: removing bad policies and leaders, superseding bad explanations, and recovering from disasters.
  • All triumphs are temporary. To use this fact to reinterpret progress as ‘so-called progress’ is bad philosophy because we know that if we strive for better explanations, we will get better at solving these too.
  • Prevention and delaying tactics are useful, but they can be no more than a minor part of a viable strategy for the future.
  • So we need the capacity to deal with unforeseen, unforeseeable failures. For this we need a large and vibrant research community, interested in explanation and problem-solving. We need the wealth to fund it, and the technological capacity to implement what it discovers.
  • Lack of wealth for Babbage made our progress stall even when he had the idea.
  • CO2 emissions never took into account the fact that we would discover and harness nuclear power. Climate change activists don’t take into account the satellites that we can put in space to reflect sunlight at will. These are few examples of pessimism and discrediting our ability to create good explanations.
  • Its hard to predict human future and that must be understood as that and that alone.
  • There is a saying that an ounce of prevention equals a pound of cure. But that is only when one knows what to prevent. No precautions can avoid problems that we do not yet foresee. To prepare for those, there is nothing we can do but increase our ability to put things right if they go wrong. Trying to rely on the sheer good luck of avoiding bad outcomes indefinitely would simply guarantee that we would eventually fail without the means of recovering.
  • Only an open ended journey of creation and exploration will save us from what lies ahead. That is the only sustainable source of safety for us.

Infinity

  • But only a starting point of an infinite adventure. All you need do is make the decision [to end your static society]. It is yours to make.’ [With that decision] came the end, the final end of Eternity. – And the beginning of Infinity. – Isaac Asimov, The End of Eternity (1955)
  • Earth is smaller in terms of the space that we understand now.
  • What we know is still nowhere near what we can know. Yet, time and again, people think the knowledge that they possess is fairly close to the limit of what is knowable. Even Feynman thought that we were at crux and already towards the closed end of what can be discovered and known.
  • Future is not yet imaginable, so very exciting in that regards.
  • Even just from 1894, we know about space time, electromagnetism, cosmology, computation and so on. Even the people who thought that their generations had discovered the crux of it led to more discoveries in the future. A future they could never even have imagined.
  • If people thought of it like that, perhaps no one would need to be reminded that science claims neither infallibility nor finality. Such an important thing.
  • So, knowledge is going from problems to better problems.
  • Prophetic fallcy has always been strong even in the community that appreciates scientific attitude.
  • Infinite ignorance is a necessary condition for there to be infinite potential for knowledge.
  • The quest for good explanations is “open ended, and infinite”.
  • No need to choose nihilism over ambiguity as an answer. Scientific attitude doesn’t need to mean 100% truth. It needs to be understood as quest for good explanations.
  • We are not denying that some problems are fundamental and we are not able to create good explanations for that. It doesn’t mean we shouldn’t be working on them, or we have saturated in our ability to create good explanations.
  • One aspect is the ancient tension between the discrete and the continuous. Just like the tension between quantum theory and general theory of relativity.
  • Is there a bound on the number of computational steps that a computer can execute during the lifetime of the universe? If there is, then physics will also impose a bound on the amount of knowledge that can be created – knowledge-creation being a form of computation.
  • Everyone’s first thought was that unbounded knowledge-creation is possible only in a universe that does not recollapse. However, on analysis it turned out that the reverse is true: in universes that expand for ever, the inhabitants would run out of energy. But the cosmologist Frank Tipler discovered that in certain types of recollapsing universes the Big Crunch singularity is suitable for performing the faster-and-faster trick that we used in Infinity Hotel: an infinite sequence of computational steps could be executed in a finite time before the singularity, powered by the ever-increasing tidal effects of the gravitational collapse itself.
  • So, when we talk about infinities, there are infinite ways to harness time and energy in such events. To the inhabitants – who would eventually have to upload their personalities into computers made of something like pure tides – the universe would last for ever because they would be thinking faster and faster, without limit, as it collapsed, and storing their memories in ever smaller volumes so that access times could also be reduced without limit. Tipler called such universes ‘omega-point universes’. At the time, the observational evidence was consistent with the real universe being of that type.
  • A small part of the revolution that is currently overtaking cosmology is that the omega-point models have been ruled out by observation. Evidence – including a remarkable series of studies of supernovae in distant galaxies – has forced cosmologists to the unexpected conclusion that the universe not only will expand for ever but has been expanding at an accelerating rate. Something has been counteracting its gravity.
  • We do not know what. Pending the discovery of a good explanation, the unknown cause has been named ‘dark energy’. Depending on what dark energy turns out to be, it may well be possible to harness it in the distant future, to provide energy for knowledge-creation to continue for ever.
  • There are many different explanations of the bounded or unbounded nature of knowledge creation based on what we understand from Physics.
  • Because the Big Bang happened a finite time ago, and because of the finiteness of the speed of light, we shall only ever see a finite portion of infinite space – but that portion will continue to grow for ever.
  • Light becomes fainter as it spreads out: there are fewer photons per unit area. That means that ever larger telescopes are needed to detect a given object at ever larger distances. So there may be a limit to how distant – and therefore how unlikely – a phenomenon we shall ever be able to see. Except, that is, for one type of phenomenon: a beginning of infinity. Specifically, any civilization that is colonizing the universe in an unbounded way will eventually reach our location.
  • We should really understand all our predictions as implicitly including the proviso ‘unless the creation of new knowledge intervenes’.
  • To attempt to predict anything beyond the relevant horizon is futile – it is prophecy – but wondering what is beyond it is not.
  • When wondering leads to conjecture, that constitutes speculation, which is not irrational either. In fact it is vital.
  • For instance, we know from universality that AI is attainable by writing computer programs, but we have no idea how to write (or evolve) the right one.
  • What is the difference between laws that are instantiated in physical reality and those that are not?
  • What is the difference between a computer simulation of a person (which must be a person, because of universality) and a recording of that simulation (which cannot be a person)? When there are two identical simulations under way, are there two sets of qualia or one? Double the moral value or not?
  • The world remains as mysterious to us as it was to Eratosthenes though the amount of good explanations might have increased 1000 folds.
  • The world is explicable. We don’t live in a senseless world.
  • There are higher levels of emergence and higher levels of explanation. Profound abstractions in mathematics, morality and aesthetics are accessible to us. Ideas of tremendous reach are possible. But there is also plenty in the world that does not and will not make sense until we ourselves work out how to rectify it. Death does not make sense. Stagnation does not make sense. A bubble of sense within endless senselessness does not make sense. Whether the world ultimately does make sense will depend on how people – the likes of us – chose to think and to act.
  • Many people have an aversion to infinity of various kinds. But there are some things that we do not have a choice about. There is only one way of thinking that is capable of making progress, or of surviving in the long run, and that is the way of seeking good explanations through creativity and criticism. What lies ahead of us is in any case infinity. All we can choose is whether it is an infinity of ignorance or of knowledge, wrong or right, death or life.
  • The better we come to understand phenomena remote from our everyday experience, the longer those chains of interpretation become, and every additional link necessitates more theory.

Behind it all is surely an idea so simple, so beautiful, that when we grasp it – in a decade, a century, or a millennium – we will all say to each other, how could it have been otherwise? John Archibald Wheeler, Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, 480 (1986

item.title: A Confession
item.description: A confession is about Leo Tolstoy’s journey into a void of emptiness that he felt during his mid 20s and then after his 50s. His seeking into the idea of why a man lives at all is very interesting with a letter he has at the very end. When a man achieves everything he aspired for, all the big dreams achieved, he gets to ask the question: what to live for now? The philosophical speculation into why we live and what we hold onto to live is revealing. There is a lot to learn from his confession to find meaning in life, to be able to live a life that’s new every day, and put despair at bay.

item.title: Tao Te Ching
item.description:
Theme #1 Teachings on non-action

Less and less do you need to force things, until finally you arrive at non-action. When nothing is done, nothing is left undone

There is nothing to be done because it all accumulates to nothing in the very end. If you start to do something, there will always be something more to do. If nothing is done, then there is nothing left to be done as well. This is metaphorical where you need to understand that you wouldn’t have anything to do in this state; not just choosing to not do anything though you want to do it. This is non-action.

item.title: Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid
item.description:
Notes

  • In order for a canon theme to work, a melody has to function in different parts yet make sense as a whole. It must first be part of a melody, and secondly a harmonization of same melody.

Bach and Braid in music

  • Ways music was canonized:
    • Copies of theme staggered in time
    • Copies of theme staggered in time as well as pitch. e.g. If a voice starts at C, another second overlapping voice can start at G which is 5 notes higher. Third voice then can start after next 5 notes at D.
    • Speed of voices can speed up. e.g. Second voice gets twice as fast.
    • Speed of voices get slower. e.g. Second voice is twice as slow as first voice.
    • Invert and make it jump up and down exactly as the original theme.
    • Play the theme backwards in time. Comes from peculiarities of crab canon.
    • Based on one theme which gets played in different voices and different keys, and occasionally at different speeds or upside down or backwards.
    • Bach wrote a fugue for the king with text note: “As the modulation rises, so may the King’s glory.”
      • Music can go infinitely recursively.

Escher and Braid in drawings

  • Escher’s drawings to show infinite recursion.
  • Escher’s drawings:
    • Strange Loops: A picture of picture which contains itself.
    • Print Gallery
    • Drawing Hands

Godel and Braid in mathematics

  • Epimenides Paradox explains how just stating a statement can create violations in logical system. This liar paradox has helped prove the properties of our current mathematical system.
  • Godel found out that mathematics was incomplete by proving that some statements in mathematics cannot even be proved.
    • “All consistent axiomatic formulations of number theory include undecidable propositions.”
  • The grand conclusion of Principia Mathematica started by Bertrand Russell is that the system is incomplete as proven by Godel. Godel’s incompleteness theorem
  • Kurt Godel showed that provability is a weaker notion than truth, no matter what axiomatic system is involved.

Highlights

Contracrostipunctus

item.title: The Prophet
item.description:
• Deep Philosophy on general terms of life. The details as he navigates each term is awesome.
  • Collection of Poem from Khalil Gibran.

Favorite lines

In today’s world, you spend 80% of your time working. Hence this is even more important in today’s time. I would like to work as if work is my prayer, else meditate.

Work is love made visible. And if you cannot work with love but only with distaste, it is better that you should leave your work and sit at the gate of the temple and take alms of those who work with joy

item.title: The Root Stanzas of the Middle Way
item.description:
Written by Nagarjuna The Buddhist Monk Madhyamka is not :

  1. Mystical doctrine concerned with otherworldly revelations. Neither it is philosophical explanation of reality.
  2. Nihlisim. Though it says pheonomena are empty, their functional effectiveness on experiential level is never questioned.

What’s the overall summary?

Goal
Liberation of beings
Method
Correct our mistaken apprehension of phenomena and to dissolve our long-ingrained belief that they exist in the way they appear.

Truth of the phenomena isn’t found to be in none of the four “ontological” extremes : existence, nonexistence, both existence and nonexistence, and neither nonexistence nor existence.

item.title: How to Live
item.description:
Author: Derek Sivers

Don’t be a part of any group. Don’t take sides on any fight. Instead of standing out from the crowd, just avoid and ignore the crowd

To be part of society is to lose a part of yourself. Cut ties with society. Don’t engage. Don’t even rebel, because that’s reacting

Don’t align with any religion, philosophy, or political stance. Stay unlabeled and unbound

Never agree with anything the same day you hear it, because some ideas are persuasively hypnotic. Wait a few days to decide what you really think

item.title: The Manual- Stoic Philosophy
item.description:
• If you have a favorite cup, remember that it is only a cup that you prefer-if it is broken, you can bear it.
  • In preparing for any action, remind yourself of the nature of the action.
  • When you are feeling upset, angry, or sad, don’t blame another for your state of mind. Your condition is the result of your own opinions and interpretations.
  • Don’t take satisfaction in possessions and achievements that are not your own. If a horse were to say, “I am handsome,” his pride may be excusable. But if you boast, " I have a handsome horse," you are claiming merit that is not yours.
  • In a voyage when ship is anchored and you go ashore for supplies, you may amuse yourself with collecting some seashells and pretty stones but your thought is still alert for captain’s call. You may need to drop your treasures and run back to the boat at any time. Likewise is life, you need to remain steadfast in pursuing your mission, always willing to shed distractions.
  • Don’t wish that all things will go well with you, but that you will go well with all things.
  • The only thing that can impede your will is your will itself.
  • If you meet temptation, use self-control; if you meet pain, use fortitude; if you meet revulsion, use patience.
  • Don’t say of anything " I have lost it, " but rather “I have given it back.”
  • For as long as the SOURCE entrusts something to your hands, treat it as something borrowed, like a traveler at an inn.
  • Stop making excuses like , “If I don’t cling tightly to my money and possessions, I’ll end up on the street. "
  • Along this path of philosophy:
    • Don’t strive to be celebrated for anything.
    • If you are praised by yourself, be skeptical for yourself. For it is no easy feat to hold onto your inner harmony while collecting accolades. While grasping for one, you are likely to drop for other.
  • Sympathize with a grieving person. Don’t just push your thoughts to others. Cry with them. Your tears will be outward, not inward.
  • When it comes across a “bad omen”, distinguish between reality and interpretation. Remind yourself that everything points to good luck if I interpret it that way. Whatever life brings, I can use it to my advantage.
  • Continually remind yourself that you are a mortal being, and someday you will die. This will inspire you to not waste your time on fruitless activities, like stewing over grievances and striving after possessions.
  • If you find yourself acting to impress others, or avoiding action out of fear about what they might think, you have left the path. Find satisfaction in following your philosophy. If you want to be respected, start by respecting yourself.
  • Find your significance within yourself. Within your own sphere of power-that is where you have the greatest consequence. Can you really give someone happiness and satisfaction-things that are in their own spheres of power and not yours? And can you give someone something that you, yourself, don’t even have?
  • If you can acquire riches without losing your honor and self-respect, then do it. But if you lose what is dearest to you, no amount of money can make up for it.
  • Do you envy someone who is popular at work, invited to parties, and spoken of in social circles? If they attract love because of positive character qualities, be glad for them. If they attract attention because of negative character qualities, be glad that you don’t have them.
  • Don’t expect to equal anyone in effect without putting forth a similar effort. A person who rarely leaves home, who doesn’t converse with, praise, and encourage others, will not attract friends.
  • Do you have anything good in place of the invitation? Yes-you have the pleasure of not making small talk with people you don’t really like, not praising someone you don’t admire, and not mingling with lackeys.
  • You ought to react in the same way you did when it was your neighbor’s property that was damaged.
  • If someone tried to take control of your body and make you a slave, you would fight for freedom. Yet how easily you hand over your mind to anyone who insults you. When you dwell on their words and let them dominate your thoughts, you make them your master.

Vocation

  • Fancying yourself to be a gladiator, orator or a philosopher but never beginning training in earnest means you are a dabbler who samples many fields, but when the time comes to commit to one, you move on to the next.
  • To find your vocation, first consider your talents and inclinations. Do you have the back, shoulders, and thighs of a wrestler? Or the potential and determination to gain them through exercise?
  • Whatever your vocation, pursue it wholeheartedly. Consider, choose, and commit.

Duties

  • Duties are determined by relations. If a man is your father, relationship implies the duties of listening to his counsel, following his instructions, patiently receiving his correction, and helping to take care of him in his old age.
  • Fulfill your duties to the best of your ability.
  • Before judging anyone’s behavior look to your own. If he insults or rejects you, don’t stoop to his level and retaliate in anger.

Circumstances

  • If you suppose events to be good or evil in themselves, when life doesn’t go as you wish you will inevitably blame the author.
  • When you understand that the outside events don’t touch your deepest self- what matters is your interpretation and reaction - you can use any circumstance to your benefit.

Behaving in public

  • Be the same person in public as in private.
  • Avoid idle chatter. Refuse to participate in gossip- tearing down, inflating, and judging other people.
  • Among friends, shift the conversation to worthy topics; among strangers, stay silent.
  • Avoid taking oaths as much as possible.
  • If a friend tells you that someone has criticized or insulted you, say, “They must not know about my other faults, or they would have pointed out those, too”.
  • Avoid extremes of elation at a win and devastation at a loss.
  • Keep your language free of obscenities. Don’t dip into the gutter in search of cheap laughs.
  • If you are unsure of how to act in a given social situation, ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would behave. Model yourself after the wisest.
  • If you win the adoration of others by pretending to be someone you’re not, you may gain high status- but you will lose out on the fulfillment of a life best suited to your attributes and qualities.

Desires

  • Consider the cost of pursuing potential pleasure, every consequence that may follow from acquiring or experiencing it, and how you will feel about it the next day.
  • Consider how you will feel about yourself tomorrow if you resist the temptation today.
  • Once you let your appetite exceed what is necessary and useful, desire knows no bounds.

Thinking

  • Watch for obstacles and errors in your line of thought.
  • Tread carefully, taking care not to stumble to illogic and unreason.
  • Whenever someone helps or hinders you, or praises or criticizes you, remember that they see you only through the lens of their own impressions. If they act or speak from a warped perspective, they hurt themselves- not you.
  • For if someone mistakes truth for falsehood, the truth is not harmed, but only the person deceived. Keep this in mind, gently turn away any insult or injury. “It seems right to them, though they are mistaken”.

Body and Mind

  • Care for your body as needed, but put your main energies and efforts into cultivating your mind.

Tit for tat

  • Everything has two handles: one by which it can be carried, and one by which it cannot. If a friend treats you unfairly, don’t try to grasp the situation by the handle of retribution- it will burn your hand.

Illogical Conclusions

  • “I am richer than you, so I am more valuable than you.”
  • “I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am superior to you.”

Logical Conclusions

  • Examples:
    • “I am richer than you, so I can buy more things than you.”
    • “I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is more polished than yours.”
    • Does a person bathe quickly? Don’t say that they bathe poorly, but only quickly.
    • Does a person drink a lot of wine? Don’t say that they drink badly, but only in abundance.
  • Unless you perfectly understand other’s motives, how can you judge them? Don’t mistake your impressions for the whole truth.

Reacting to others

  • If anyone calls you ignorant and says you know nothing, be sure that you are now a true student of philosophy.
  • Sheep don’t spit out grass to show the farmer how much they’ve eaten- they ruminate on it, digest it, and then display the results in wool and milk.
  • Once you have reigned in your bodily appetites, don’t brag about it. Ask for water, but don’t announce at the table, “I only drink water.”
  • Don’t make a spectacle of self-deprivation. When you fast, tell no one.

Philosophy

  • First topic of philosophy is practical application of principles.
  • Second topic is understanding the reasons behind the principles.
  • Third topic is verifying the principles through logic.
  • Philosophy is for living, not just learning.
